nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Shallow, clear water lets light reach the corals and algae on the atolls, driving photosynthesis on the reef.

nodes.name: Sulu Sea currents
nodes.desc: Ocean currents move water, larvae and plankton across the isolated atolls and carry them to the reef edges.

nodes.name: Nutrients
nodes.desc: Dissolved nutrients from mixing water and recycled waste are scarce in tropical seas and limit algae and plankton.

nodes.name: Bacteria & microbes
nodes.desc: Break down dead coral tissue, algae, plankton and animal remains, returning nutrients to the water.

nodes.name: Phytoplankton
nodes.desc: Drifting microscopic algae at the base of the open-water food chain, eaten by zooplankton.

nodes.name: Reef-building corals
nodes.desc: Hard corals that build the reef and host symbiotic algae; they feed partly on sunlight and partly on plankton. Habitat for most reef species.

nodes.name: Halimeda and reef algae
nodes.desc: Calcified green algae that grow on reef rock and sand, grazed by reef fish and turtles.

nodes.name: Zooplankton
nodes.desc: Tiny drifting animals that graze phytoplankton and feed fusiliers and manta rays.

nodes.name: Bumphead parrotfish
nodes.desc: A large reef fish that scrapes and crunches live coral and algae; its feeding produces coral sand and clears space on the reef.

nodes.name: Surgeonfish
nodes.desc: Algae-grazing reef fish that keep algae from overgrowing coral.

nodes.name: Green sea turtle
nodes.desc: A grazing turtle that eats algae and seagrass and nests on the sandy islets of the atolls.

nodes.name: Hawksbill turtle
nodes.desc: A reef turtle that eats mainly sponges plus algae and other reef animals; it also nests on the atoll islets.

nodes.name: Crown-of-thorns starfish
nodes.desc: A starfish that feeds on live coral; outbreaks can strip large areas of reef, and one was reported at Tubbataha in 2009.

nodes.name: Fusiliers
nodes.desc: Schooling fish that feed on zooplankton in the water above the reef, and are prey for larger predators.

nodes.name: Reef manta ray
nodes.desc: A filter-feeding ray that strains zooplankton from the water and visits reef cleaning stations.

nodes.name: Napoleon wrasse
nodes.desc: A large, endangered reef wrasse that eats molluscs, crustaceans, fish and toxic prey including crown-of-thorns starfish.

nodes.name: Giant trevally
nodes.desc: A powerful reef predator that hunts fish in the reef and lagoon.

nodes.name: Brown noddy
nodes.desc: A tropical seabird that nests on the atoll islets and catches small fish at the sea surface.

nodes.name: Brown booby
nodes.desc: A plunge-diving seabird that nests on the islets and feeds on fish and squid.

nodes.name: Whitetip reef shark
nodes.desc: A reef shark that rests in caves by day and hunts reef fish, octopus and crustaceans at night; Tubbataha is noted for very high densities of it.

nodes.name: Hammerhead sharks
nodes.desc: Hammerheads are reported in the park, which records eleven shark species, and hunt fish and squid around the reef.

nodes.name: Tiger shark
nodes.desc: A large shark reported at Tubbataha and named among its top predators; it eats fish, turtles and many other prey.
